questions.prompt: Which of these operators can only be overloaded as a member function?
options: `operator+`
`operator<<`
`operator=`
`operator==`
`operator!`
questions.explanation: Assignment, function call, subscript and `->` must be member functions; every class already has an implicitly declared copy assignment operator, and a free `operator=` is rejected outright. The others may be members or non-members. `operator<<` is tempting because it is usually a non-member, but that is a convention forced by the stream being the left operand, not a rule in either direction.

options: Well-formed: addition is commutative, so the compiler swaps the operands
Ill-formed: no `operator+` accepts an `int` on the left and a `V` on the right
Well-formed: `2` is converted to `V` and the member is called on it
Well-formed only since C++20, which adds reversed candidates for `+`
questions.explanation: A member `operator+` makes the left operand the implicit object argument, so it only matches `V + int`. The compiler never swaps the operands of `+`; C++20 reversed candidates exist only for `==` and the relational operators via `<=>`. Converting `2` to `V` is not possible here, and user-defined conversions are never applied to the implicit object argument anyway.

options: `k=0`, `2` only; an explicit call to the postfix form is ill-formed
`k=5`, `1`; `c++` calls the prefix overload
questions.explanation: The `int` parameter only distinguishes postfix from prefix. When the postfix form is invoked through `c++`, the standard says it is called with the argument zero. Calling `operator++` by name is an ordinary member function call, so you may pass any `int`, here 5. Each call increments `n` once, so the final value is 2.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what does this program print?
options: `f`, `0`: `g()` is skipped because the left operand is false
`f`, `g`, `&&`, `0`, but `f` and `g` may appear in either order
`g`, `f`, `&&`, `0`: function arguments are evaluated right to left
questions.explanation: An overloaded `&&` is a function call, and both arguments are evaluated before the body runs, so there is no short-circuit. Since C++17, [over.match.oper] sequences the operands of an overloaded operator in the order prescribed for the built-in one, so `f()` is evaluated before `g()`. The third option describes the pre-C++17 rule, when the order was unspecified.

options: Nothing: ill-formed, because `operator->` must return a pointer
`Outer->`, then `42`
`Outer->`, `Inner->`, then `42`
Nothing: ill-formed, because `Inner` has no member `x`
questions.explanation: `o->x` is interpreted as `(o.operator->())->x`. The result is an `Inner` lvalue, which is a class type, so `->` is applied to it again, calling `Inner::operator->`, which yields a `Raw*`, and the built-in `->` finishes the job. `operator->` may return any class type that itself supports `->`; only the final step must produce a pointer.

options: Well-formed: `12` is converted to `long double` and `d` is 12000
Ill-formed: an integer literal never selects the `long double` literal operator
Well-formed, but `d` has type `unsigned long long`
Ill-formed: literal operators must be declared `constexpr`
questions.explanation: The literal operator is chosen from the kind of literal, with no conversions. For the integer literal `12_km`, lookup tries `operator""_km(unsigned long long)`, then the raw form taking `const char*`, then a numeric literal operator template; none exists, so the program is ill-formed. Writing `12.0_km` or adding an `unsigned long long` overload fixes it. `constexpr` is optional.

questions.prompt: Which of these operators cannot be overloaded?
options: `,` (comma)
`co_await`
questions.explanation: The pointer-to-member operator `.*` is on the short list of operators that cannot be overloaded, with `::`, `.` and `?:`. Its sibling `->*` can be overloaded, as an ordinary binary operator with no drill-down. The comma, `co_await` and `&&` are all overloadable, although overloading the comma or `&&` loses the built-in short-circuit behaviour.

options: Ill-formed: `operator()` cannot be a static member function
Ill-formed: `operator[]` cannot have a default argument
Ill-formed: a subscript expression needs at least one operand
questions.explanation: C++23 (P1169 and P2589) allows `operator()` and `operator[]` to be static member functions, and P2128 lets `operator[]` take any number of parameters, including zero, with default arguments. So `Grid{}(3, 4)` is 12 and `Grid{}[]` uses the default 7, giving 19. Each of the other options was true in C++20.
